analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks that let U.S. companies pay lower taxes by shifting profits and operations overseas.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 17 Democratic senators, never left the Senate Finance Committee and received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: U.S. companies today can pay much lower tax rates on money earned through foreign subsidiaries than on money earned at home. This bill would end that gap: companies would pay the full U.S. rate on foreign profits in the year they are earned, could no longer stack up foreign tax credits to zero out their U.S. bill, and could no longer dodge U.S. taxes by paper-shuffling their headquarters abroad or loading up debt in the U.S. company. It also treats foreign corporations that are actually run from the United States as American companies for tax purposes.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in two ways: the government would collect more revenue from multinational corporations, and domestic businesses and their workers would no longer compete against rivals that lower their tax bill by moving profits and jobs offshore. The changes fall entirely on large companies, not on individual taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: Ends the reduced tax rate on foreign profits of U.S. companies, so income earned through foreign subsidiaries is taxed at the full corporate rate, and requires companies to include that income in the year it is earned rather than deferring it indefinitely.
Limits the foreign tax credit on a country-by-country basis, so companies cannot use taxes paid in high-tax countries to shield income parked in low-tax havens.

Caps the interest deductions a multinational group can claim in the U.S., based on the group's own consolidated financial statements, closing a common way companies shift profits out of the United States by loading debt on the U.S. side.
Tightens rules against corporate inversions, treating foreign reorganized companies as domestic if they are still majority-owned by the original U.S. owners or still run from the United States.

Treats foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic corporations for income tax, closing the door on companies that operate as American businesses but claim a foreign address on paper.

Removes tax advantages for foreign oil and gas income, including treating certain foreign oil-related income as immediately taxable and restricting carryback of foreign tax credits for oil and gas taxes.

analysis.who_pays: Large U.S.-based multinational corporations with foreign subsidiaries, companies that have moved or are considering moving their headquarters abroad to lower their taxes, foreign oil and gas operations, and multinational companies that currently deduct heavy U.S. interest expenses to reduce their U.S. tax bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: U.S. multinationals and oil and gas firms

drawbacks.text: U.S. multinationals would face a higher effective tax rate on foreign earnings than foreign competitors face in the same markets, which supporters of the current rules argue puts American companies at a disadvantage when competing for business and investment abroad.

The country-by-country credit rules, financial-statement-based interest limits, and anti-inversion tests add significant compliance complexity and rely heavily on new Treasury regulations, and companies argue some of the changes could produce double taxation of the same income.
Higher taxes on corporations are partly passed through to workers and consumers over time, according to standard economic analysis, so some share of the cost would not stay with shareholders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks specific, well-documented tax advantages of moving profits, debt, and headquarters offshore, and its costs fall almost entirely on large multinationals rather than individual taxpayers. The main real tradeoff is the competitiveness argument and the risk of double taxation, which the bill partly addresses but not perfectly. The bigger flaw is not design but fate: it was never seriously considered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on February 9, 2023, and the committee never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, joined by 16 Democratic cosponsors, including Sens. Durbin, Warren, Booker, and Casey.
All 16 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that is the last action in the record.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and oil and gas companies kept the lower effective tax rates on foreign profits, offshore interest deductions, and foreign-address structures the bill would have eliminated. No member of the public gained anything, since the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinationals that kept offshore tax advantages

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the No Tax Breaks for Outsourcing Act in the Senate on February 9, 2023.

for.name: 16 Democratic senators (Durbin, Van Hollen, Duckworth, Hirono, Booker, Warren, Reed, Heinrich, Blumenthal, Murphy, Baldwin, Markey, Casey, Merkley, Schatz)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; no Republican did.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup, hearing vote, or committee vote appears in the record before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsors and made no attempt to advance the bill, leaving it entirely within the committee of a chamber whose agenda it did not support.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican ever signed on, and with a Democratic-held but closely divided Senate and Republican-held House, the bill never moved past referral.

industries.industry: U.S. multinational corporations with foreign subsidiaries
industries.note: The bill ends the reduced rate on foreign profits, requires current-year inclusion, restricts foreign tax credits to a country-by-country basis, and caps U.S. interest deductions using the group's own financial statements. Its gain is the public's cost in forgone revenue and a tilted playing field against domestic-only businesses.

The bill treats foreign base company oil-related income as immediately taxable and eliminates the carryback of foreign tax credits for oil and gas taxes, raising taxes on foreign oil and gas operations.

industries.industry: Companies that relocate headquarters abroad (corporate inversions)
industries.note: Tighter inversion rules treat foreign reorganized companies as domestic if they remain majority U.S.-owned or U.S.-managed, and foreign corporations run from the United States become taxable as domestic. Keeping paper headquarters abroad would stop producing a tax advantage.
